questions.question: Draw a cross-section of Earth and label the four layers: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
Use color or labels to show which layers are solid and which are liquid.
Show how the crust is different under the ocean and under a continent.
Sketch convection currents in the mantle. Use arrows to show where material rises and sinks.
Draw Earth's magnetic field. Label the layer that helps create it.
Draw a divergent boundary. Use arrows for plate movement and label what forms.
Draw an ocean plate meeting a continental plate. Label the trench and the volcanoes.
Draw two continental plates colliding. What landform forms?
Draw a transform boundary with arrows for plate movement. Add a star where earthquakes happen.
Draw an earthquake and label the focus and the epicenter.
Draw the water cycle. Label evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.
Show where the energy for the water cycle comes from.
Add transpiration, runoff and groundwater to your water cycle.
Draw a mountain where one side gets lots of rain and the other side is dry. Explain with arrows.
Draw the rock cycle. Label igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock and the processes that connect them.
Show how an igneous rock can become a sedimentary rock.
Draw layers of sedimentary rock. Label the oldest layer.
Draw where heat and pressure make metamorphic rock.
Sketch magma cooling slowly underground and quickly at the surface. Show the crystal sizes.
Draw a cold front from the side. Show the warm air, cold air and where storms form.
Draw a warm front from the side.
Draw a high pressure and a low pressure system. Use arrows for the wind.
Draw how air moves in a sea breeze on a sunny afternoon.
Place Earth at the right spot in its orbit for each season in the northern hemisphere. Then draw an arrow showing which way Earth’s axis tilts.
Drag each label onto the layer of Earth it names. Then draw an arrow to the hottest layer.
Place each moon where it is in its orbit when we see that phase from Earth. The Sun’s light comes from the left.
Put an arrow on each plate and turn it to show how the plates move at a convergent boundary: the plates move toward each other. Then draw what you might see at the surface.
Put an arrow on each plate and turn it to show how the plates move at a divergent boundary: the plates move away from each other. Then draw what you might see at the surface.
Put an arrow on each plate and turn it to show how the plates move at a transform boundary: the plates slide past each other. Then draw what you might see at the surface.

Match up the fossil and mountain evidence to put the 8 continents back together as Pangaea. The pieces may not fit exactly. Then draw a line along the mountain belt that runs from piece to piece.
Key: gray = European flora, pink = Cynognathus, blue = Lystrosaurus, orange = Glossopteris, green = Mesosaurus, light green with triangles = mountains.
Fit South America and Africa together so the fossil colors line up: pink Cynognathus, orange Glossopteris and green Mesosaurus. Then draw a line linking each matching pair.
Sort each clue by the kind of evidence for continental drift.

Was each clue found by Wegener or after Wegener?

questions.question: Drag each label onto the right place on the sea floor. The oldest sea floor is on the right.
Draw arrows to show which way the plates move at the ridge. Shade the oldest rock and label where new rock forms.
Draw how Pangaea broke apart. Show the continents before and after, and add an arrow for the way each one moved.
What could make the continents move? Draw arrows in the mantle that could carry the plates, and label what powers them.
The continents do not fit together perfectly today. Draw a coast then and now, and label what changed it.
Show what happens when the ocean plate meets the continent. Add arrows for the way each plate moves, then label the trench and where volcanoes form.
Add a star everywhere earthquakes happen along this boundary. Where are the deepest ones?
Label the vent, magma chamber, crater and lava. Then draw arrows to show how magma moves.
Draw the focus and the epicenter of an earthquake on this fault. Then add arrows showing which way each block of rock moved.
Draw the waves spreading out from the focus. Where would the shaking be the strongest?
Draw arrows for evaporation, condensation, precipitation and runoff. Label each one.
Show where the energy for the water cycle comes from and where water is stored.
Draw a plant cell and label at least 5 organelles.
Draw an animal cell. Label the nucleus, cell membrane and mitochondria.
Draw two structures that only plant cells have.
Show a substance moving across the cell membrane by diffusion. Use arrows.
Draw a food chain with 4 organisms. Use arrows to show the flow of energy.
Draw a food web with at least 2 producers and 2 consumers.
Draw what happens to the web if the top predator is removed.
Draw an energy pyramid and show how much energy moves up each level.
Draw the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas.
Show what happens to the particles when ice melts.
Draw the energy transformations on a roller coaster from the top of the first hill to the bottom.
Draw a light ray reflecting off a mirror. Label the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection.
Draw a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb.
Plot (2, 3), (4, 7) and (6, 11) and connect them. What is the slope?
Draw a number line from -5 to 5 and plot -3, 0.5 and 4.
Sketch a speed-vs-time graph of a car that speeds up, cruises, then stops.
Graph y = 2x + 1.
Draw fraction bars to model 3/4 + 1/2.

Sort each word by its part of speech.
